The safe region for dissection is the plane between the gallbladder itself and the overlying fatty and areolar tissue. The hook cautery instrument is appropriately positioned, elevating this yellowish fatty tissue off the gallbladder neck. This plane, located in the center of the image, is the correct area to develop in order to achieve the Critical View of Safety. The serosal surface of the gallbladder body, being retracted by the grasper on the left, is also a safe surface to work on, but the primary safe dissection zone is where the hook is actively creating a window.

The unsafe regions are extensive in this view. The entire right side of the image, showing the dark red liver parenchyma, is unsafe to cut as it would cause bleeding and liver injury. More critically, the area inferior and medial to the hook—the thick, yellowish band of tissue in the lower half of the image—is the most dangerous zone. This area contains the un-identified structures of the hepatocystic triangle, namely the cystic duct, cystic artery, and potentially the common bile duct or an aberrant hepatic artery. Dissection in this region without definitive identification of these structures carries a high risk of catastrophic bile duct or vascular injury.

The boundary between safe and unsafe is precisely at the tip of the dissecting hook. The surgeon is safely creating a plane by staying on the gallbladder wall. Any deviation deeper or more medially from this point enters the unsafe zone. The goal of this dissection is to safely expose the structures within the unsafe zone so they can be positively identified before ligation and division.
